findings.situation: A filer has a fruit or nut tree or vine, either one placed in service in 2025 that must use straight line, or a specified plant planted or grafted in 2025 that they elected under section 168(k)(5) to take the special allowance on; none of the listed items covers either case, so a truthful filer answers no.
findings.source_text: i4562 p. 11: "The straight line method is the only applicable method for trees and vines bearing fruits or nuts." i4562 p. 6: "the special depreciation allowance only applies for the first tax year in which the plant is planted or grafted. The plant will not be treated as qualified property eligible for the special depreciation allowance in the subsequent tax year in which it is placed in service."
findings.why: The question only reaches straight line when the filer elected it, and does not mention the specified-plant allowance, which is taken in the planting year rather than the placed-in-service year. Such a tree or vine stays in the tool, which would apply the default 10-year method or the allowance in the wrong year.

findings.situation: A filer converted property held for personal use to business or income-producing use; the list covers conversion to personal use but not conversion from personal use, so the filer answers no.
findings.source_text: i4562 p. 11, Column (b): "If you converted property held for personal use to use in a trade or business or for the production of income, treat the property as being placed in service on the conversion date." i4562 p. 14: "your basis for depreciation is the smaller of the property's adjusted basis or its fair market value on the date of conversion."
findings.why: Converted property has its own placed-in-service date and its own basis rule (the lower of adjusted basis or fair market value). The question does not screen it out, so the tool would depreciate it from cost and the original purchase date.

findings.situation: A filer marries mid-year (not in December), and each spouse's separate Form 1095-A shows 12 uniform months in columns A and B, but the applicable SLCSP premium for the combined coverage family changes in the month of marriage.

findings.why: The question is asked per form, and its list of reasons column B can be wrong leaves out marriage, so the filer would truthfully answer yes for each form. Line 10 needs No because the applicable SLCSP premium is not the same every month, so monthly lines 12–23 are required.

findings.situation: A filer had solar property installed on a newly built home in 2024 but first moved in during 2025, so the instructions treat the costs as paid in 2025; under the question's rule (installation completed in 2024) the filer would answer No.
findings.source_text: i5695 (2025) p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins." The same applies to reconstruction: "when your original use of the reconstructed home begins."
findings.why: The question says a cost counts "when its original installation is completed" and leaves out the construction and reconstruction rule. A filer in this situation truthfully answers No, so Schedule 3 line 5a is forced to zero and the credit is lost.

findings.situation: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose association or corporation paid for qualifying solar or battery property in 2025 may answer No because they paid nothing directly.

findings.why: The question asks only whether "you" had 2025 costs, and the help does not mention the proportionate share of association or cooperative costs. An ordinary filer could truthfully answer No and lose the Part I credit.

findings.situation: A filer whose only 2025 costs are for the construction of a new home, or for doors, windows or insulation at a home that is not their main home, answers yes. Line 32 then stays at zero, but the line 32a or 32b checkbox can be checked even though no credit is claimed.

findings.situation: A couple divorced under a final decree in late 2025 only so they could file as unmarried, and they intend to and do remarry each other in 2026; the filer truthfully answers that they were unmarried at the end of 2025.
findings.source_text: p501 p. 6, Divorce and remarriage: "If you obtain a divorce for the sole purpose of filing tax returns as unmarried individuals, and at the time of divorce you intend to and do, in fact, remarry each other in the next tax year, you and your spouse must file as married individuals in both years."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer was unmarried at year end and does not mention this rule. The truthful answer is Yes, but the text treats the filer as married, so household.hoh_eligible must not be true.

findings.situation: A filer in a registered domestic partnership or civil union, which is not denominated as a marriage under state law, is asked whether they were 'unmarried' at the end of 2025.
findings.source_text: p501 p. 6, Definition of marriage: "Individuals who have entered into a registered domestic partnership, civil union, or other similar relationship that isn't denominated as a marriage ... aren't lawfully married for federal tax purposes"
findings.why: The question does not say how such relationships are treated. An ordinary partner could reasonably answer No, seeing the partnership as a marriage, or Yes, seeing themselves as legally unmarried. The text requires Yes.

findings.situation: A filer received nonqualified deferred compensation or nongovernmental section 457 plan income that is included in box 1 of their Form W-2 or box 1 of Form 1099-NEC, but the employer or payer did not show it in W-2 box 11, in W-2 box 12 with code Z, or in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 95, Line 20, item 5: "If you received income from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan or nongovernmental section 457 plan that is included in box 1 of your Form W-2, or in box 1 of Form 1099-NEC, don't include that income on line 8 of the worksheet. The income should be shown in (a) box 11 ... If it isn't, contact your employer or the payer for the amount of the income."
findings.why: The text triggers the special case when the income is included in box 1 of the W-2 or 1099-NEC, whether or not it is shown in the other boxes. The question defines the income only as 'an amount in box 11 ... box 12 with code Z, or in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC'. A filer whose forms leave those boxes blank would answer no, so the return is not refused even though the worksheet's line 8 would overstate compensation.

findings.situation: An excess amount sits in this person's traditional IRA because of an employer contribution or an improper rollover, not because of the person's own 2025 contribution, and was not withdrawn by the due date.
findings.source_text: p590a (2025) p. 35: "An excess contribution could be the result of your contribution, your spouse's contribution, your employer's contribution, or an improper rollover contribution."
findings.why: The first bullet asks only whether "your contributions for 2025 to traditional and Roth IRAs" exceeded the limit. A filer whose excess came from an employer contribution or a rollover that did not qualify would truthfully answer no, yet the 6% tax on Form 5329 applies.

findings.situation: On a joint return, a spouse with little or no taxable compensation contributed up to $7,000 ($8,000 if 50 or older) to a spousal IRA, which the other spouse's compensation supports.
findings.source_text: Question: "or more than your taxable compensation"; i1040gi (2025) p. 95, Line 20: "But you, or your spouse if filing a joint return, must have had earned income to do so."
findings.why: Read literally, the question has the nonworking spouse answer yes because the contribution is more than "your" taxable compensation. On a joint return the combined compensation supports the contribution, so there is no excess, and the yes wrongly refuses the return.

findings.situation: A filer whose W-2s show code G 457(b) deferrals together with code D 401(k) deferrals adds them as the question says ('the total ... from all your employers') and answers yes. For example, $15,000 D plus $15,000 G is more than $23,500, yet the 401(k) amount alone is within its limit.
findings.source_text: iw2w3 p. 20: "Code G—Elective deferrals and employer contributions (including nonelective deferrals) to any governmental or nongovernmental section 457(b) deferred compensation plan"; "when using code G for section 457(b) plans, include both elective and nonelective deferrals"
findings.why: The question has the filer total every box 12 deferral against one 401(k) figure of $23,500. Box 12 code G also holds 457(b) amounts, including employer nonelective contributions, which are not tested against that 401(k) limit. A truthful total can therefore give a yes when there is no excess deferral.

findings.situation: A filer whose W-2 box 12 shows prior-year USERRA make-up deferrals (for example 'D 23 2250.00, D 24 1250.00') includes them in the 'Form W-2 box 12' total and answers yes because of contributions that belong to other years.
findings.source_text: iw2w3 p. 20: "If any elective deferrals ... during the year are make-up amounts under ... (USERRA) for a prior year, you must enter the prior-year contributions separately ... D 23 2250.00, D 24 1250.00. A 2025 contribution of $7,000 does not require a year designation"
findings.why: The question points the filer to the box 12 amounts without telling them to leave out entries marked with a prior year. Those make-up amounts are not 2025 deferrals, so counting them can produce a 2025 excess that does not exist.

findings.situation: A filer who deferred under plans of two unrelated employers, each within the limit but over $23,500 combined, may rely on the help text and answer no because neither plan administrator reported an excess.
findings.source_text: Question help: "Your plan administrator tells you if you deferred more than the limit." iw2w3 p. 20: "Even though the 2025 limit ... is $23,500, Alex's total elective deferral amount of $26,500 is reported in box 12 with code D"
findings.why: The question asks for a total 'from all your employers', but the help suggests the plan administrator decides whether there is an excess. An administrator only sees its own plan, so the filer can reasonably read the question two ways that give different answers.

findings.situation: A distribution coded 2 where the stated exception does not apply to any of it, for example a payer coded separation at age 55 but the filer left service before that year; the filer answers no because the exception does not cover 'only part' of it.
findings.source_text: i5329 p. 1, Who Must File: "...but box 7 of your Form 1099-R doesn't indicate an exception or the exception doesn't apply to the entire distribution."; i5329 p. 5, Line 2: "Enter on line 2 the amount that you can exclude."
findings.why: When a code 2 exception wholly fails, the Line 2 exclusion and exception number are wrong just as when it partly fails. The gate needs a yes here, but the wording asks only about an exception covering part of the distribution.

findings.situation: A filer under 59½ receives a code 7 distribution from a governmental section 457 plan (not from a rollover) and answers yes because they were under 59½, although the additional tax does not apply and the code is not wrong.
findings.source_text: Question: "its code is wrong because you were under age 59½ when you received it (code 7)"; i5329 p. 5, exception 13: "Distributions from a section 457 plan, which aren't from a rollover from a qualified retirement plan."
findings.why: The wording treats being under 59½ as proof that code 7 is wrong. This brings in distributions that properly carry code 7 and owe no early-distribution tax, so they are refused unnecessarily.

findings.situation: A code 7 recipient under 59½ can read the clause either as 'answer yes whenever I was under 59½' or as 'answer yes only if I believe the code is actually wrong.'
findings.source_text: Question: "or its code is wrong because you were under age 59½ when you received it (code 7)"
findings.why: The two readings give different answers for the same facts. The help shown ("Married filing separately and unsupported items are refused with citations") does not settle which reading is meant.

locators: p. 1, Who Must File, "You received a distribution subject to the tax on early distributions from a qualified retirement plan (other than a Roth IRA) and you meet an exception to the tax on early distributions from the list shown later, but box 7 of your Form 1099-R doesn’t indicate an exception or the exception doesn’t apply to the entire distribution."

findings.situation: An Alaska parent applied for a dependent child's dividend and had it deposited into the parent's own account, so the parent could reasonably count the child's dividend as 'paid to you'.
findings.source_text: p525 (2025) p. 31: "If you received a payment from Alaska's mineral income fund (Alaska Permanent Fund dividend), report it as income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8g. ... The state of Alaska sends each recipient a document that shows the amount of the payment with the check."
findings.why: The text ties line 8g to the recipient named on the state's document, which is the child, not the parent. The question's 'paid to you (and ... your spouse)' does not say to leave out dividends of children or other dependents, even when the payment went to the parent's account. A filer could read it either way and enter different amounts on line 8g, which flows into line 9.

findings.situation: A filer rents out personal property (for example, occasionally renting out a boat) without a profit motive, so the rental is an activity not engaged in for profit; the question's carve-out 'not the rental of personal property' tells the filer to leave this income out, even though line 8j needs it.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8l: 'Income from the rental of personal property if you engaged in the rental for profit but were not in the business of renting such property'; p525 p. 31: 'You must include on your return income from an activity, even if you don't expect to make a profit from that activity... Enter this income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j.'
findings.why: Line 8l covers only personal-property rentals engaged in for profit, so a rental not engaged in for profit is income from an activity not engaged in for profit and belongs on line 8j. The question's blanket exclusion of 'the rental of personal property' drops it, and no other listed input picks it up.

findings.situation: A filer has a section 179 carryover from a year before 2024 but did not file a Form 4562 for 2024, for example because the business had no depreciation or new property that year, so the carryover was never shown on a 2024 line 13.
findings.source_text: i4562 (2025) p. 5, Line 10: "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation. If you filed Form 4562 for 2024, enter the amount from line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562."
findings.why: The instructions define the carryover as all disallowed amounts from previous years and use the 2024 line 13 only as the source when a 2024 form was filed. The question asks only for the 2024 line 13 amount, zero if none, so this filer would answer zero and lose a carryover that line 12 needs.

findings.situation: A filer with two or more Schedules C that use the simplified home-office method has one combined 2024 carryover, and the tool adds that whole amount to each business's own 2025 elections.
findings.source_text: i4562 (2025) p. 5, Line 12: "The limitations on lines 5 and 11 apply to the taxpayer, and not to each separate business or activity... you may allocate your allowable section 179 expense deduction among them." The question asks for "The carryover of disallowed section 179 deduction from line 13 of your (and, on a joint return, your spouse's) 2024 Form 4562".
findings.why: The question collects the taxpayer's total carryover, but sc.ho_s179_max treats it as the carryover for this one business. The same carryover is then counted once for every Schedule C, which overstates each business's section 179 amount used in the simplified-method limit.

findings.situation: A filer who had more than one business in 2024 filed a "Summary" Form 4562 plus a separate Form 4562 for each business, so there are several 2024 forms with a line 13.
findings.source_text: i4562 (2025) p. 5, Line 12: "enter 'Summary' at the top of Part I of the separate Form 4562 you are completing for the total amounts from all businesses or activities... On line 12 of the Form 4562 you prepare for each separate business or activity, enter the amount allocated..."
findings.why: "line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562" could be read as the Summary form's line 13, or as one business's form, or as a sum across all the forms. These readings give different amounts, and summing could double count if the Summary form is included.

locators: p. 5, Line 10, "If you filed Form 4562 for 2024, enter the amount from line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562" (owner: the printed amount)

findings.situation: A filer whose Form 1098 mortgage interest is subject to the debt or use limits (for example, mortgage debt above the limit, or a loan not used to buy, build, or improve the home) must still enter the limited, deductible portion on line 8a, but the question only asks for interest 'when no debt or use limit applies'.
findings.source_text: f1040sa 2025 p.1, line 8a: "Home mortgage interest and points reported to you on Form 1098. See instructions if limited"; line 8: "If you didn't use all of your home mortgage loan(s) to buy, build, or improve your home, see instructions and check this box"
findings.why: Line 8a covers limited filers too; they enter the deductible amount figured under the instructions. The question excludes them, so a truthful limited filer gives zero or nothing, and line 8e loses their deductible Form 1098 interest. No gate or refusal is listed that sends these filers elsewhere.

findings.situation: A filer whose interest is limited reads 'after confirming the debt/use limits do not apply' together with 'Zero if none'. One reading is to enter zero. Another is to enter the full Form 1098 amount anyway. A third is to enter the limited amount.
findings.source_text: Question help: "Home mortgage interest and points reported to you on Form 1098, when no debt or use limit applies. Zero if none." vs. f1040sa 2025 p.1, line 8a: "See instructions if limited"
findings.why: The wording does not say what to enter when a limit does apply. Reasonable filers would give different values: zero, the full amount, or the limited amount.

findings.situation: A filer had a section 965(i) triggering event during 2025 without a transfer agreement, so the triggered deferred net 965 tax liability must be added on line 16 (box 3, "965INC"), but the question's list never names it.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 36: "Triggering event under section 965(i). If you had a triggering event under section 965(i) during the year and did not enter into a transfer agreement, check box 3 and enter the amount of the triggered deferred net 965 tax liability and enter \"965INC\" on the line next to that box."
findings.why: The filer is left to recognise this as an "additional Form 1040 line 16 tax" from the generic opening words alone, since the list omits it. A truthful No lets the tool compute line 16 without the tax.

findings.situation: A filer born on January 1 (2008, 2007 or 2002) reads their age at the end of 2025 as one year younger than the instructions treat it, and answers Yes for Form 8615 when it is not required (for example, born 1/1/2002 and a full-time student, or born 1/1/2008 with earned income over half of support).
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 36: "A child born on January 1, 2008, is considered to be age 18 at the end of 2025; a child born on January 1, 2007, is considered to be age 19 at the end of 2025; and a child born on January 1, 2002, is considered to be age 24 at the end of 2025."
findings.why: The question says "you were under 18 at the end of 2025, or 18 with earned income of not more than half your support, or a full-time student 19 to 23" without the January 1 birthday rule. These filers answer Yes and the return is refused although Form 8615 does not apply.

findings.situation: A filer whose vehicle is a truck or van placed in service after July 6, 2003 and specially modified into a qualified nonpersonal use vehicle (for example, shelving, front bench only, company advertising) answers no, so the tool computes it as a passenger automobile under the listed-property limits.
findings.source_text: i4562 p. 15: "The following vehicles are not considered passenger automobiles. ... Any truck or van placed in service after July 6, 2003, that is a qualified nonpersonal use vehicle." Also i4562 p. 3: "Listed property does not include: ... 4. Any truck or van placed in service after July 6, 2003, that is a qualified nonpersonal use vehicle."
findings.why: The list refuses the other excepted vehicles (transport for hire, ambulance, hearse) but leaves out qualified nonpersonal use trucks and vans. These vehicles are neither passenger automobiles nor listed property, so the passenger-automobile limits and the qualified-business-use test do not apply to them, and the gate should refuse them.

findings.situation: A vehicle whose business plus investment use was over 50% in an earlier year, but whose qualified business use that year was 50% or less, can get either answer depending on how the filer reads the two bullets.
findings.source_text: Question: "its business use was 50% or less in any earlier year" and "its qualified business use is 50% or less once you leave out uses that are not qualified business use". p463 p. 25: "You must meet this more-than-50%-use test each year of the recovery period" and "It doesn't include use for the production of income (investment use)".
findings.why: The earlier-year bullet says "business use" without the qualified-business-use exclusions. The qualified-use bullet uses the present tense "is", which reads as 2025 only. A filer could therefore count earlier-year investment or related-person use as business use and answer no, even though the text treats a year at 50% or less of qualified business use as forcing straight-line depreciation and recapture.

findings.situation: A filer whose employer paid tips in two jobs, one on the tipped-occupation list (such as server) and one not on it, gets a Form W-2 box 7 that covers both, and the question tells them the amount is 'taken from one of these', including box 7.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 103: 'If you received tips as an employee in more than one occupation for the same employer, only those tips that were received in an occupation on the list of occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, are considered qualified tips. Do not include tips received in occupations that are not included on this list in line 4a, 4b, or 4c.'
findings.why: The question says 'Qualified tips from this employer, taken from one of these (your choice): Form W-2 box 7...', and neither it nor its help explains the occupation limit. One filer will copy the box 7 total, while another will enter only the listed-occupation share, so the two give different column (b) amounts.

findings.situation: A gambling dealer (TTOC 201) receives tips in casino chips or other tokens that can be exchanged for a fixed amount, and truthfully answers no because chips are not 'cash, check, card or app'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 102: "paid in a cash medium, including by cash, check, credit card, debit card, gift card, tangible or intangible tokens that are readily exchangeable for a fixed amount (for example, casino chips), and any other form of electronic settlement or mobile payment app"
findings.why: The question defines cash only as 'cash (including by check, card or app)'. It leaves out tokens such as casino chips, which the text counts as a cash medium. A filer whose tips are all qualified may therefore answer no, and tipjob.mixed is set to true when it should be false.

findings.irs_text: f1099div p. 5: "But, if no amount is shown in boxes 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2f and your only capital gains and losses are capital gain distributions, you may be able to report the amounts shown in box 2a on your Form 1040"

findings.who: A filer, or the spouse on a joint return, whose only Form 1099-DIV comes from a fund that paid no ordinary dividend that year. Box 1a is blank and only box 2a shows a long-term capital gain distribution, with part of it in box 2b or 2d.
findings.why_no: The box 2a helper applies only 'when you or your spouse received dividends or other distributions'. If the tool reaches it through a parent question about dividends, the filer may answer no, because a capital gain distribution does not feel like a 'dividend'. Then box 2a is zero, the gate is false, and boxes 2b, 2c, 2d and 2f are never asked.
findings.irs_text: f1099div p. 5: 'Box 2a. Shows total capital gain distributions from a regulated investment company (RIC) or real estate investment trust (REIT).' and 'Box 2b. Shows the portion of the amount in box 2a that is unrecaptured section 1250 gain...'
findings.fix: Word the parent question as whether you or your spouse received any Form 1099-DIV, or any amount in any of its boxes (including capital gain distributions in box 2a). Do not ask about 'dividends' alone.

findings.who: A shareholder of a REIT or RIC that kept its long-term capital gains and sent Form 2439, not a Form 1099-DIV box 2a. The Form 2439 shows unrecaptured section 1250 gain or 28% rate gain.
findings.why_no: Box 2a of Form 1099-DIV is truly zero, so the gate is false. The lines here are defined only by 1099-DIV boxes, so this filer's amounts of the same kinds must come from a separate Form 2439 path.
findings.line: div.box2b_if_capital_gain, div.box2d_if_capital_gain (by kind of gain, not by document)
findings.irs_text: f1099div p. 5: 'Box 2b. Shows the portion of the amount in box 2a that is unrecaptured section 1250 gain... See the Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain Worksheet in the Instructions for Schedule D (Form 1040).'
findings.fix: No change is needed to this gate, because each box 2b, 2c, 2d and 2f amount is by definition a portion of box 2a and is zero when box 2a is zero. Make sure Form 2439 amounts are collected elsewhere and feed the same Schedule D worksheets.
